result.markdown: # Tutorial 4: Inference and tests against zero {#b-ep04} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 4, you can - construct and interpret intervals for a mean and a proportion; - complete two-sided tests of zero-valued contrasts; - connect a test decision with its confidence interval; - interpret the t distribution, degrees of freedom, errors, and power; - explain when a one-sided alternative is legitimate and why the exam is two-sided; - read a regression coefficient test without overclaiming. ::: Tutorials are **exam preparation sessions**: every task below follows the format of the final exam. The standing routine for each task is the same --- the TA states the task, pairs work on it first for a few minutes with AI use allowed, and the solution is then discussed in plenary, starting from the pair attempts. This tutorial covers Lectures 9--10: the t distribution and intervals from Lecture 9, testing decisions and one-sided alternatives from Lecture 10. Exam tests are two-sided. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Bring your after-class work from Lectures 9 and 10. Review [Mathematics Refresher: intervals, degrees of freedom, and standardisation](../resources/math-refresher.html) if needed. Use the cumulative formula sheet through Lecture 10. Write from memory: 1. the t confidence-interval form; 2. the t statistic for testing a mean contrast against zero; 3. why the critical value comes from the t distribution rather than the normal, and the meaning of $df=n-1$; 4. the definition of a two-sided p-value; 5. the 95%-interval/5%-test decision link. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. $\widehat\delta\pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\delta)$. 2. $T=\widehat\delta/\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\delta)$. 3. The population SD is replaced by the sample SD $S$, which itself varies across samples; the heavier-tailed t distribution prices in that extra uncertainty. Estimating the sample mean leaves $n-1$ freely varying deviations for estimating spread. 4. Under $H_0$, the probability of a statistic at least as far from zero as the observed statistic in either direction. 5. For matched two-sided t procedures, reject zero exactly when the 95% interval excludes zero. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In class Attempt every task before opening its answer. Every conclusion must name the parameter, units, population, direction, and evidence limit. All tasks use the reproducible seed-123 sample of 100 and the equity gap, built exactly as in Lectures 7 and 9: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) set.seed(123) sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE) pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ] pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp <- pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct - 15 ``` ::: ### Task 1 --- Mean contrast For the reproducible sample, define $$ D=\text{initial equity offered}-15. $$ 1. Calculate $\bar d$, $s_d$, the SE, and the degrees of freedom. 2. Construct a 95% interval for $\delta=E[D]$. 3. Test $H_0:\delta=0$ against $H_1:\delta\ne0$. 4. Explain why the interval and test agree. 5. Explain why the critical value comes from `qt(0.975, df = 99)` rather than `qnorm(0.975)`. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp n <- length(d) d_bar <- mean(d) s_d <- sd(d) se_d <- s_d / sqrt(n) critical <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1) ci_d <- d_bar + c(-1, 1) * critical * se_d t_value <- d_bar / se_d p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = n - 1) c(estimate = d_bar, sd = s_d, se = se_d, df = n - 1, lower = ci_d[1], upper = ci_d[2], t = t_value, p_value = p_value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` estimate sd se df lower upper -2.240000000 7.707886555 0.770788656 99.000000000 -3.769411916 -0.710588084 t p_value -2.906114385 0.004515396 ``` ::: ::: $\bar d=-2.24$, $s_d=7.7079$, $SE=0.7708$, and $df=99$. The 95% interval is approximately $(-3.77,\,-0.71)$. The statistic is $t=-2.906$ and the two-sided p-value about 0.0045, so reject the zero-gap null. The interval excludes zero because it uses the same t model and SE as the test. The critical value is a t quantile because $\sigma$ was estimated by $s_d$; with $df=99$ the value 1.984 is only slightly above the normal 1.96, but the t choice is the correct procedure. ::: ### Task 2 --- Proportion contrast Define $\delta_p=p-0.50$, where $p$ is the finite-frame deal proportion. 1. Estimate $\delta_p$. 2. Perform a two-sided large-sample z-test against zero. 3. Construct the course's large-sample 95% interval for $p$ and translate it into an interval for $\delta_p$. 4. State why the test and interval SEs differ. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- nrow(pitch_sample) phat <- mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show) p0 <- 0.50 delta_hat <- phat - p0 null_se <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n) z_value <- delta_hat / null_se p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_value)) estimated_se <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n) ci_p <- phat + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * estimated_se ci_delta <- ci_p - p0 c(phat = phat, estimated_gap = delta_hat, z = z_value, p_value = p_value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` phat estimated_gap z p_value 0.640000000 0.140000000 2.800000000 0.005110261 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(proportion_lower = ci_p[1], proportion_upper = ci_p[2], gap_lower = ci_delta[1], gap_upper = ci_delta[2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` proportion_lower proportion_upper gap_lower gap_upper 0.54592 0.73408 0.04592 0.23408 ``` ::: ::: $\hat p=0.64$, so $\widehat\delta_p=0.14$. Under the null, $SE_0=0.05$, $z=2.80$, and the two-sided p-value is about 0.005. Reject the zero-gap null. The proportion interval is approximately $(0.546,\,0.734)$, corresponding to a gap interval $(0.046,\,0.234)$. The test calculates variation under $p_0$ --- how surprising the sample is in the null's world --- while the interval estimates it with $\hat p$, making no null assumption. ::: ### Task 3 --- Read a regression coefficient row Suppose a model of initial equity offered reports: | Predictor | Estimate | SE | t | p-value | 95% interval | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Amount requested, per $100,000 | -0.290 | 0.058 | -5.00 | <0.001 | (-0.403, -0.177) | 1. State the tested hypotheses. 2. Explain every number in units. 3. Give the statistical conclusion at 5%. 4. State two claims the row cannot justify. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The test is $H_0:\beta_{ask}=0$ against $H_1:\beta_{ask}\ne0$. The estimate says that another \$100,000 requested is associated with 0.290 percentage points less fitted initial equity, holding the model's other predictors fixed. The SE measures sampling uncertainty in the same coefficient units. The statistic is $-0.290/0.058=-5.00$. The p-value is below 0.001, and the 95% interval excludes zero, so reject the zero-coefficient null. The row alone does not establish causality or show that the model's assumptions hold. ::: ### Task 4 --- Errors and power For Task 3: 1. describe a Type I error; 2. describe a Type II error; 3. state how a larger sample affects SE and power; 4. explain why raising $\alpha$ is a trade-off rather than a free gain. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer A Type I error is concluding that the population-model ask coefficient differs from zero when it equals zero. A Type II error is failing to reject zero when a specified non-zero coefficient is true. A larger independent sample usually reduces the SE and raises power. Raising $\alpha$ also raises power, but it increases the Type I error probability by exactly the same mechanism: a wider rejection region catches more of everything. ::: ### Task 5 --- One-sided alternatives and the exam convention Task 1 gave $t=-2.906$ with $df=99$ and a two-sided p-value of about 0.0045. 1. Calculate the p-values for the pre-specified one-sided alternatives $H_1:\delta<0$ and $H_1:\delta>0$. 2. A student who saw the negative estimate first proposes to report the left-sided p-value "since the direction is now known." Explain the error. 3. State the course's exam convention and one reason behind it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer Left-sided: $P(T_{99}\le-2.906)\approx0.0023$, the single left tail. Right-sided: $P(T_{99}\ge-2.906)\approx0.9977$. Choosing the tail after inspecting the estimate lets the 5% rejection mass follow the data to whichever side the noise landed, which doubles the true Type I error rate to about 10%; the alternative must be fixed by the research question before the sample is examined. Exam convention: all tests are two-sided, both because business questions usually make either direction relevant and because the convention removes the temptation of tail-picking. ::: ### Task 6 --- Repair the conclusion Critique: > The coefficient is significant, so asking for more money causes founders > to offer less equity, and there is less than a 0.1% chance that the null > is true. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The p-value is not the probability that the null is true, and significance does not establish causality. A defensible conclusion reports a negative adjusted association, its magnitude and interval, the evidence against a zero coefficient under the model, and the observational design and assumption limits. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class ### Timed individual practice --- 25 minutes Redo this unassisted and against the clock: no notes, no AI, formula sheet only --- exam conditions. A random sample of 81 customers gives mean spending 42 euros, sample SD 9 euros, and 54 renewals. 1. Define $\delta_\mu=\mu-40$, construct its 95% interval (use $t_{0.975,80}\approx1.99$), and test a two-sided zero null. 2. Define $\delta_p=p-0.60$, construct the course's 95% interval, and test a two-sided zero null. 3. State the Type I error for each test. 4. Explain why the mean result is only just significant while the estimated mean difference is still 2 euros. 5. Write a six-sentence report separating estimate, uncertainty, decision, practical importance, population, and causality. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model answer For the mean, $\widehat\delta_\mu=2$, $SE=9/\sqrt{81}=1$, and $df=80$. With $t_{0.975,80}\approx1.99$, the gap interval is approximately $(0.01,\,3.99)$, equivalent to a mean interval $(40.01,\,43.99)$. The statistic is $t=2.00$ and the two-sided p-value is about 0.049, so reject the zero mean-gap null just narrowly. For renewal, $\hat p=54/81=0.667$. The estimated gap is 0.067. The large-sample proportion interval is approximately $(0.564,\,0.769)$, so the gap interval is $(-0.036,\,0.169)$. Under $H_0:p=0.60$, $SE_0\approx0.0544$, $z\approx1.22$, and the two-sided p-value is about 0.22; do not reject. A Type I error would be claiming a non-zero mean spending gap when $\mu=40$, or a non-zero renewal gap when $p=0.60$. The mean result is borderline because the 2-euro estimate is almost exactly two SEs from zero --- precision, not size, drives the p-value. A complete report must still evaluate whether a 2-euro difference matters and whether the sampling design supports the intended population claim. Neither test identifies a causal explanation. ::: ### Check your understanding Complete from memory: 1. A 95% confidence interval is correctly described as ... 2. Reject $H_0$ at 5% exactly when the matched 95% interval ... 3. A Type I error is ...; power is ... 4. A one-sided alternative is legitimate only when ... 5. A regression coefficient row tests ... ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. The product of a procedure that captures the fixed parameter in about 95% of repeated valid samples --- never "a 95% chance the parameter is inside." 2. Excludes zero (for matched two-sided procedures using the same SE). 3. Rejecting a true null; the probability of rejecting when a specified alternative is true. 4. It is fixed before the data are inspected and follows from the research question. (Exam tests are two-sided.) 5. $H_0:\beta_j=0$ against $H_1:\beta_j\ne0$, holding the model's other predictors fixed. ::: ### Make it yours (5 minutes) :::: {.utility-prompt} Utility: two sentences Think of your EiA venture --- or any business you know well. Take the one claim about it that you would most like to defend in front of an investor, and write two sentences: first phrase it as a zero-contrast test with a realistic sample and state which error --- the false alarm or the missed effect --- would cost you more, then say what interval outcome would make you change a real decision rather than just a slide. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## See an example, then write your own Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. "The claim I must defend: average order value equals the €9 break-even, tested two-sided on my next 150 orders. The missed effect would cost me more --- walking away from a viable business --- so an interval sitting entirely above €9 would make me order packaging stock, not just update a slide." ::: You can discuss this task --- and any other task in this tutorial --- with **Tilly**, the course AI assistant on Canvas. :::: QM Basic is complete. Next, use the QM Basic Formula Sheet and attempt the QM Basic Mock Exam. Continue to QM Intermediate when that course begins. :::
